newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says it plans to boost nuclear exports.
newsitem.headline: Russia says it plans to boost nuclear exports.

text.p: Nuclear Energy Minister Viktor Mikhailov said on Monday that Russia, its nuclear industry facing financial crisis and a growing anti-nuclear lobby at home, would increase exports of nuclear technology.

Mikhailov, in a clear response to criticism from the United States, defended a controversial nuclear deal with Iran. He also pledged that Moscow would finish the construction of nuclear plants in China and press ahead with similar plans in India.

"Export should be increased. We cannot solve the problems by dividing countries into ones that are loved and ones that are not loved...This would only stimulate terrorism," Mikailov told a news conference.
"It is better to be friends and to cooperate."

Mikhailov said 150 Russian constructors were already working in Iran helping it build a VVER-440 reactor. Tehran wants Moscow to construct four more units but Mikhailov said this would be possible only after resolving unspecified financial problems.
Experts have put the cost of the Iran project, which the United States opposes because it accuses Tehran of sponsoring international terrorism, at about $2 billion.
In north-west China, he said, Russia had completed construction of the first part of a plant for enriching uranium and finalised details on the building of two 1,000-megawatt nuclear reactors.
Mikhailov said Beijing wanted to build four more reactors some time in the future.
"Now there are some problems with payments (from India) but I think that we will sign an agreement with India later this year," Mikhailov said.
He told Reuters that the cost of the China project was estimated at $3-4 billion, while the cost of building the nuclear plant in India was $2-3 billion.

One nuclear ministry official told Reuters that Russia had been negotiating with Indonesia on supplies of nuclear reactors which can be based on ships and with Cuba on completion of a nuclear station.
The official said Moscow was also also discussing sales of nuclear technology to Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Vietnam.
Nuclear power accounts for about 12 percent of the electricity generated in Russia.
Most new projects have been delayed since the 1986 Chernobyl disaster in Ukraine, which was then part of the Soviet Union, but some of the planned stations are already being built.
Moscow recently announced plans to shut down 18 ageing nuclear reactors by the year 2010.
Mikhailov criticised Russian anti-nuclear campaigners who last month won an unprecedented referendum in the central region of Kostroma against construction of a nuclear station there.
"We don't plan to construct new reactors...where people are against it. Kostroma has done so -- that is its right," he said.
But he added: "We will fight the greens. They are the most extremist part of the population..no one will stop progress."
Mikhailov complained about a lack of financing from the state budget but said that last month his ministry had reduced its backlog of wages from four months to 1-1/2 months.

The avarage monthly salary in the nuclear industry is one of the highest in Russia -- 1.2 million roubles (about $240), but Mikhailov said it would be increased to 1.5 million roubles ($300) later this year.
Mikhailov said that military programmes accounted for 10 percent of Russia's nuclear industry, compared to one-third in the Soviet days.
